entry: Organochloride insecticide, notable for its environmental impacts. DDT was first synthesized in 1874. Its insecticidal action was discovered in 1939 by Swiss chemist Paul Hermann Müller. It was used in [[World War II]] to limit the spread of [[Malaria|malaria]] and typhus. Rachel Carson's *Silent Spring* (1962) cited claims that its agricultural use threatened wildlife, particularly birds, and in 1972 the United States banned DDT's agricultural use. A worldwide agricultural ban followed under the Stockholm Convention, which exempts public health use within [[World Health Organization]] guidelines.

American rapper, songwriter and actor, born Earl Simmons. Regarded as one of the greats of [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], he signed with Ruff Ryders Entertainment after an unsuccessful tenure on [[Columbia Records]]. His debut album, *It's Dark and Hell Is Hot* (1998), sold 251,000 copies in its first week. He was the first artist to have his first five albums consecutively debut atop the Billboard 200, and he sold over 75 million records worldwide. He acted in *Exit Wounds* (2001) alongside [[Steven Seagal]] and *Cradle 2 the Grave* (2003) alongside [[Jet Li]].

Technique for determining an individual's [[DNA]] characteristics, also called DNA fingerprinting. In forensic investigations it compares suspects' profiles with DNA evidence. Modern techniques are highly reliable, but they give only a fallible probabilistic estimate of a match. British geneticist Sir Alec Jeffreys discovered the technique in 1984 at the University of Leicester, after realizing that some regions of DNA contain highly variable repetitive sequences unique to each individual. Although 99.9% of human DNA sequences are the same in every person, the variable regions allow individuals to be distinguished unless they are [[Twin|identical twins]]. DNA profiling is also used in paternity testing, to establish immigration eligibility, and in genealogical and medical research. Its first forensic use, in the murders of two teenagers in Narborough, Leicestershire, led to the conviction of Colin Pitchfork in January 1988.

Process by which a cell makes exact copies of its [[DNA]]. It occurs in all organisms and is essential to inheritance, cell division and the repair of damaged tissues. Because each original strand serves as a template, every replicated molecule contains one original strand and one newly synthesized strand. Replication usually begins at origins of replication, where [[Enzyme|enzymes]] called helicases unwind the double helix and replication forks grow in both directions. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides that complement the template strand. Proofreading and error-checking mechanisms ensure near-perfect fidelity, with an error rate as low as one in 10⁹ nucleotides. Replication occurs during the S (synthesis) stage of interphase. It can also be performed *in vitro*, as in the [[Polymerase chain reaction|polymerase chain reaction]] (PCR).

Digital optical disc data storage format. It was invented in 1995 and first released on November 1, 1996, in Japan. It has the same dimensions as a [[Compact disc|compact disc]] but stores far more data: up to 4.7 GB on a standard single-layer disc, 8.5 GB on a dual-layer disc and 17.08 GB on a dual-layer, double-sided disc. DVDs are used for video (DVD-Video), software and data storage, and rewritable formats include DVD-RW, DVD+RW and DVD-RAM. Popular for distributing films in the 2000s, the format was the dominant home video medium until the rise of streaming and higher-capacity [[Blu-ray]] discs.

American singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist, regarded as a pioneer of the neo-soul movement. His debut album, *Brown Sugar* (1995), was certified platinum. His second album, *Voodoo* (2000), debuted at number one on the U.S. Billboard 200, and its single "Untitled (How Does It Feel)" won the Grammy Award for Best Male R&B Vocal Performance. After struggles with depression, drug addiction and [[Alcoholism|alcoholism]], he released *Black Messiah* (2014), which won Best R&B Album at the 58th Grammy Awards. He died of [[Pancreatic cancer|pancreatic cancer]] while producing a fourth album.

Unidentified hijacker of 1971. On November 24, 1971, a man using the alias Dan Cooper hijacked Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 305, a [[Boeing]] 727 flying from Portland, Oregon, to [[Seattle]]. He demanded $200,000 in ransom and four [[Parachute|parachutes]], released the passengers in Seattle, and parachuted from the aircraft over a remote, heavily wooded area of southwestern Washington. A reporter's error gave him the name D. B. Cooper. In 1980, $6,000 of the ransom was found near the [[Columbia River]]. The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] (FBI) pursued the case for 45 years, but his identity and fate remain unknown. The hijacking prompted metal detectors at airports and mandatory baggage inspection.

Ceylonese statesman, first Prime Minister of Ceylon (1947–52). He led the independence movement that established self-rule in Ceylon and is considered the "Father of the Nation". As a student he excelled at [[Cricket|cricket]]. After joining the family business, he managed the family estates and the Kahatagaha [[Graphite]] Mine. With his brothers he was active in the temperance movement, which grew into the independence movement after the 1915 Sinhalese-Muslim riots, and was imprisoned without charges for 46 days. He was elected unopposed to the Legislative Council in 1924 and to the State Council in 1931, where he served as Minister of Agriculture and Lands. He was elected to the first Parliament of Ceylon and formed a government as Prime Minister.

American film director, considered one of the most influential figures in the history of motion pictures. He pioneered many aspects of film editing and expanded the art of the narrative film. He is known mainly for *The Birth of a Nation* (1915), one of the most financially successful films of all time, which has also been denounced for its portrayals of African Americans and its glorification of the [[Ku Klux Klan]]. The film led to riots in several U.S. cities, and the NAACP attempted to have it banned. With [[Charlie Chaplin]], [[Mary Pickford]] and Douglas Fairbanks, he founded United Artists in 1919 to let actors and directors make films on their own terms. By the time of his final feature, *The Struggle* (1931), he had made nearly 520 films, including nearly 480 short movies.

Japanese [[Zen]] Buddhist monk, writer and philosopher who founded the Sōtō school of Zen. Originally ordained in the Tendai school, he was dissatisfied with its teaching and traveled to [[China]], where he trained under Tiāntóng Rújìng, a teacher of the Cáodòng lineage of Chinese Chan. On his return to [[Japan]] he promoted *zazen* (sitting meditation) through works such as *Fukanzazengi* and *Bendōwa*. He founded Eihei-ji, one of the two head temples of the Sōtō school, in present-day Fukui Prefecture. His magnum opus, the *Shōbōgenzō* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye), and the *Eihei Shingi*, the first Japanese Zen monastic code, remain central sources for the contemporary Sōtō Zen tradition.

Illusion of memory of having already experienced the present situation. Approximately two-thirds of surveyed populations report experiencing it at least once. The term was first used in 1876 by French philosopher Émile Boirac. It is associated with temporal lobe [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]] and with migraines with aura, while early attempts to link it to [[Anxiety|anxiety]], [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]] and other [[Mental disorder|mental disorders]] found no correlations of diagnostic value. It is more commonly reported by people who travel often, watch films or remember their dreams.

City (pop., 2025: 619,444), capital of [[North Rhine-Westphalia]], Germany. It is the seventh-largest city in Germany and lies mostly on the right bank of the [[Rhine]]. It is the central city of the Rhine-Ruhr region, the second-biggest metropolitan region by GDP in the European Union. It gained city rights in 1288 after the Battle of Worringen and became capital of the newly created state in 1946. An international business and fashion center, it is headquarters to two Fortune Global 500 companies, and Messe Düsseldorf organizes nearly one-fifth of premier trade shows. Its academy of arts has included [[Gerhard Richter]] among its members. The city has a large [[Japan|Japanese]] community, and its Rhenish [[Carnival]] ranks third in Germany after those of [[Cologne]] and Mainz.

City and port in central [[Vietnam]], the fourth-largest city in the country by population and one of its nine centrally governed cities. Its port, location on National Route 1 and the North–South Railway make it a transport hub. Its origins lie in the kingdom of [[Champa]], established in AD 192. Known as *Cửa Hàn* ("Hàn River Estuary") during the Đại Việt period, it was called Tourane during French colonial rule from 1884 to 1945. Some sources derive its name from the Cham word *da nak*, meaning "opening of a large river". It was separated from Quảng Nam province on January 1, 1997, and a reform effective July 1, 2025, reabsorbed Quảng Nam. Its Human Development Index of 0.800 (very high) ranks fifth among Vietnam's municipalities and provinces.

Ancient Indo-European people of the region of Dacia, near the [[Carpathian Mountains]] and west of the [[Black Sea]]. Often considered a subgroup of the Thracians, they spoke the Dacian language, which may be a subgroup of Thracian. Their territory covered mainly present-day [[Romania]] and Moldova. Greek writers called them Getae, and Romans called them Daci. Under King Burebista, tribal confederations were unified around 60–50 BCE into a kingdom that threatened Roman interests. Under [[Decebalus]] they resisted the Roman emperors [[Domitian]] and [[Trajan]] in wars of AD 101–102 and AD 105–106. These ended with the fall of their capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia, and the annexation of Dacia as a Roman province. Roman sources, motivated by imperial propaganda, often portray them as savage foes, while excavations reveal advanced stone architecture and metallurgy.

International [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] art movement of the early 20th century, formed in the context of [[World War I]]. It began in 1916 in [[Zurich]], [[Switzerland]], at the Cabaret Voltaire founded by Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings, where participants protested war, nationalism and cultural conformity through nonsense, chance and ridicule. Ball is seen as the founder of the movement, and his Dada Manifesto of 1916 first collected its principles. Dada spread quickly to [[Berlin]], [[Paris]], [[New York City]] and centers in Europe and Asia. Key figures included [[Tristan Tzara]], [[Marcel Duchamp]], [[Max Ernst]] and [[Man Ray]]. Duchamp's readymades became emblematic of its anti-art stance. Dada laid groundwork for abstract art and sound poetry, influenced [[Surrealism]] and [[Pop art|pop art]], and was a prelude to [[Postmodernism|postmodernism]].

Indian film producer, director and screenwriter, widely regarded as the father of Indian cinema. His debut film, *Raja Harishchandra* (1913), was the first Indian motion picture and the first full-length Indian historical feature film. Between 1913 and 1937 he made 94 feature-length films and 27 short films, often handling editing, set design and makeup himself. Trained in [[Oil painting|oil]] and [[Watercolor painting|watercolor painting]] and in [[Photography|photography]], he adapted Indian historical stories for the screen. The [[Government of India]] instituted the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in his honor, which remains the highest award in Indian cinema.

Puerto Rican rapper, singer and songwriter, dubbed the "King of Reggaeton". Following a shooting incident, he abandoned plans for a professional [[Baseball|baseball]] career and turned to music. His album *Barrio Fino* (2004) was the top-selling Latin music album of the 2000s, and "Gasolina" is credited with introducing reggaeton to audiences worldwide. His 2017 single "Despacito", with Luis Fonsi, was the first Spanish-language song to top the Billboard Hot 100 since "Macarena" in 1996. He has sold over 30 million records worldwide.

City in southeastern [[South Korea]] and the country's third-largest urban agglomeration after [[Seoul]] and [[Busan]]. Known as "Apple City" for its [[Humid subtropical climate|humid subtropical climate]], which suits high-quality apples, and as "Textile City" for its [[Textile|textile]] industry, it was an economic engine of [[Korea]] in the 1960s–1980s. In ancient times it was part of the proto-kingdom Jinhan, and later came under the Silla Kingdom. During the [[Joseon]] period it was the capital of Gyeongsang Province. The city was given its current name in 757. Today it focuses on [[Fashion|fashion]] and high-tech industries through the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Free Economic Zone.

Metropolitan city (pop., 2015: 1,518,775) in central [[South Korea]], known as a technology and research center. It is home to 23 universities and colleges, and to research centers of chaebols such as [[Samsung]] and LG in the Daedeok Innopolis. Developed as a railway town, it lies about 50 minutes from [[Seoul]] by KTX or SRT [[High-speed rail|high-speed rail]]. From the 1980s many national administrative functions moved from Seoul to Daejeon, most now in the Government Complex. The city hosted Expo '93 and will be the main host city of the 2027 Summer World University Games. It has a [[Monsoon|monsoon-influenced]] four-season climate with wet, hot summers and drier, cold winters.

Anthropomorphic black duck, a [[Cartoon|cartoon]] character in the [[Looney Tunes]] series. Created by Tex Avery and Bob Clampett, he debuted in *Porky's Duck Hunt* (1937) and became one of the first "screwball" characters of the late 1930s. He often served as a foil to [[Bugs Bunny]] and starred in 130 golden age shorts, making him the third-most frequent character in the series. In *The Scarlet Pumpernickel* (1950) he received the middle name Dumas, a nod to [[Alexandre Dumas]]. He was voiced primarily by [[Mel Blanc]] from his debut through 1989.

French electronic music duo, formed in [[Paris]] in 1993 by Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo. They achieved popularity in the late 1990s as part of the French house movement. Their final studio album, *Random Access Memories* (2013), won five [[Grammy Awards]] in 2014, including Album of the Year and Record of the Year for "Get Lucky", featuring [[Pharrell Williams]]. Their 2016 single "Starboy", with [[The Weeknd|the Weeknd]], gave them their only number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The duo announced an amicable split in 2021 after 28 years.

Swedish economist and diplomat, second [[Secretary-General of the United Nations]] (1953–61). At 47 when elected, he was the youngest person to have held the post. He presided over the first UN peacekeeping forces, the United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF) in Egypt during the [[Suez Crisis]] and the United Nations Operation in the Congo (ONUC). He died in a plane crash while en route to cease-fire negotiations during the Congo Crisis, and he is the only posthumous recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize. U.S. president [[John F. Kennedy]] called him "the greatest statesman of our century", but his legacy is controversial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the broader Global South, given his performance during the Congo Crisis.

Republic of [[Russia]] in the North Caucasus, along the [[Caspian Sea]]. Its population of over 3.1 million includes more than 30 ethnic groups and 14 official languages, with Russian as the lingua franca. Most residents speak Northeast Caucasian or [[Turkic languages|Turkic]] languages. Makhachkala is the capital and largest city. The name is Turkic and Persian, meaning "land of the mountains". In antiquity southern Dagestan was part of [[Caucasian Albania]], which came under the [[Parthian Empire]] and then the [[Sasanian Empire]]. Its peoples converted to [[Christianity]] alongside [[Zoroastrianism]]. Dagestan is known internationally for combat sambo, and many of its fighters have turned to [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial arts]].

Short, pointed fighting [[Knife|knife]], typically with one or two sharp edges, designed or capable of being used as a cutting or thrusting weapon. Flint, bone and ivory daggers appeared in the [[Neolithic]] period, and copper daggers in the early [[Bronze Age]]. Many cultures have used adorned daggers in ritual and ceremonial contexts. Because of their use in historic weapon assemblages, daggers have associations with [[Assassination|assassination]] and murder. Some thrusting daggers, such as the stiletto of the [[Renaissance]], have no cutting edge at all. In most modern contexts a dagger has a short blade with a sharply tapered point, usually two cutting edges and a full crossguard. Because daggers are primarily weapons, knife legislation in many places restricts their manufacture, sale and possession.

Early [[Photography|photographic]] process, the first publicly available. Invented by [[Louis Daguerre]] and introduced worldwide in 1839, it used a silver-plated [[Copper|copper]] sheet polished to a mirror finish and made light-sensitive with fumes. After exposure in a camera, the latent image was made visible with [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] vapor. The image is unique and its surface is delicate. The daguerreotype was almost completely superseded by 1856 by cheaper processes such as the ambrotype. Since the late 20th century, some photographers have revived it for artistic use.
